title: Past Simple
sub: Finished actions at a finished time — yesterday, last week, in 2019.

tl.cap: One completed action, fully in the past — the moment is closed.

form.p: subject + verb-ed  ·  irregular: go → went

uses.d: The action started and finished in the past, often with a time expression.

ex.s: I lived in Japan for three years.

uses.d: Past simple carries the main events of a story, one after another.

ex.s: She opened the door, saw the cake and smiled.
First we packed, then we left for the airport.

uses.d: Did is the past helper — and the main verb goes back to base form.

mistakes.no: I didn't went to the party.
mistakes.yes: I didn't go to the party.
mistakes.why: After didn't, use the base verb.

mistakes.no: Did you saw the news?
mistakes.yes: Did you see the news?
mistakes.why: Did already shows past — see stays base.

mistakes.no: She buyed a dress.
mistakes.yes: She bought a dress.
mistakes.why: Buy is irregular: buy → bought.

tip: Past appears once per clause: either in the verb (went) or in did — never both.

q.q: They ___ to Hualien last weekend.
q.why: Last weekend → past simple; go → went.

q.q: ___ you finish your homework?
She ___ (eat) breakfast at seven this morning.
We ___ (not / watch) TV last night.

q.sent: He bought a gift for his mother
I didn't saw the message yesterday .
q.why: After didn't, the verb returns to base form.

q.sent: She teached English for ten years .

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: Where did you went last night?
Where did you go last night?
Where you did go last night?
q.why: Question: where + did + subject + base verb.

title: Past Continuous
sub: Was / were + V-ing — an action in progress at a moment in the past.

tl.cap: An action already in progress at a moment in the past — often interrupted by a shorter one.

form.p: subject + was / were + verb-ing  ·  I/he/she/it → was, you/we/they → were

uses.t: In progress at a past time
uses.d: An action that was already happening at a specific moment in the past.

ex.s: At nine o'clock, we were having dinner.
This time yesterday, I was flying to Tokyo.
It was raining when I woke up.

uses.d: A longer background action (past continuous) is cut in by a shorter one (past simple) — often with when or while.

ex.s: While I was studying, my brother was playing games.

uses.d: Add not to was/were for negatives; put was/were before the subject for questions.

mistakes.no: I was work at 8 p.m.
mistakes.yes: I was working at 8 p.m.
mistakes.why: Past continuous needs was/were + verb-ing.

mistakes.no: We was watching TV.
mistakes.yes: We were watching TV.
mistakes.why: We / you / they take were, not was.

mistakes.no: What you were doing?
mistakes.yes: What were you doing?
mistakes.why: In questions, was/were goes before the subject.

tip: The long action takes was/were + -ing (the background); the short action that interrupts it takes past simple — joined by when or while.

q.q: At nine o'clock last night, I ___ dinner.
q.why: In progress at a past time → was cooking.

q.q: We ___ watching TV when you called.
While she ___ (drive), it started to rain.
They ___ (not / sleep) at midnight.

q.sent: What were you doing at noon
He was play soccer at 4 p.m .
q.why: After was/were, use the -ing form: was playing.

q.sent: While we were eat , the phone rang .

q.q: The phone rang while I ___ a shower.
q.why: A short action (rang) interrupts a longer one → was taking.

title: Present Perfect Simple
sub: Connecting the past with now — experiences, changes and results that still matter.

tl.cap: An action or experience in an open period that reaches up to now.

form.p: subject + have / has + past participle

uses.d: Use it for things you have (or haven't) done in your life, when the exact time doesn't matter.

ex.s: She has never flown in a helicopter.

ex.n: ever = at any time in your life

uses.d: A past action with a present result — the focus is on now.

ex.s: I have lost my keys. (= I can't get in now)
He has broken his leg. (= it's still broken)
The train has just left. (= we missed it)

uses.d: For a situation that started in the past and continues to now.

mistakes.no: I have seen that movie yesterday.
mistakes.yes: I saw that movie yesterday.
mistakes.why: A finished time (yesterday) needs past simple.

mistakes.no: She has went home.
mistakes.yes: She has gone home.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle: go → gone.

mistakes.no: I live here since 2019.
mistakes.yes: I have lived here since 2019.
mistakes.why: Since + continuing situation → present perfect.

tip: Ask: is the time period closed (yesterday, last year) or open (today, this week, my life so far)? Closed → past simple. Open → present perfect.

q.q: I ___ my homework, so I can relax now.
q.why: Past action with a present result → present perfect.

q.q: She has lived in Taichung ___ 2018.
q.why: Since + a starting point in time.

q.q: Have you ever ___ (eat) sushi?
He has ___ (break) his arm — it's in a cast.

q.sent: We have known each other for years
I have visited Tokyo last summer .
q.why: Last summer is finished time → past simple: I visited.

q.sent: She has wrote three emails today .

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: Did you ever been to Japan?
q.why: Has + just + past participle is correct.

title: Present Perfect Continuous
sub: Have / has been + V-ing — an action that started in the past and is still going on now.

tl.cap: An action continuing from the past right up to now — the focus is on how long.

form.p: subject + have / has been + verb-ing
ex: I have been studying for three hours.

uses.d: An action that began in the past and is still continuing — often with for, since or how long.

ex.s: We have been waiting for an hour.
He has been learning English since he was six.

uses.t: Recent activity with a result now
uses.d: A recently finished action whose result you can still see or feel.

ex.s: My eyes hurt because I have been reading all night.
The ground is wet; it has been raining.

uses.d: Add not to have/has; put have/has before the subject in questions.

mistakes.no: I am studying since 3 o'clock.
mistakes.yes: I have been studying since 3 o'clock.
mistakes.why: From a past point up to now → present perfect continuous.

mistakes.no: She has been work here for years.
mistakes.yes: She has been working here for years.
mistakes.why: Need been + verb-ing.

mistakes.no: He has been knowing her for years.
mistakes.yes: He has known her for years.
mistakes.why: Stative verbs (know) use present perfect, not the continuous.

tip: Focus on the activity and how long → present perfect continuous (have been V-ing); focus on the finished result or the number → present perfect (have + past participle).

q.q: I ___ for two hours, and I'm still waiting.
q.why: Started in the past, still going → have been waiting.

q.q: She ___ here since 2019.
q.why: since 2019 up to now → has been working.

q.q: You look exhausted. Have you ___ (run)?
q.why: Recent activity with a present result → have you been running?

q.q: It ___ (rain) all day — the streets are flooded.

q.sent: I have been study English for years .
q.why: Need been + verb-ing: have been studying.

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: He has been knowing me for years.
I am living here since May.
They have been playing for an hour.
She has been work all day.
q.why: have/has been + V-ing; stative verbs (know) don't take the continuous.

title: Past Perfect
sub: Had + past participle — the past before the past.

tl.cap: Two past events — the earlier one takes had + past participle.

form.p: subject + had + past participle
ex: The train had left when I arrived.
She had never seen snow before that trip.

uses.t: The earlier of two past actions
uses.d: When two things happened in the past, past perfect marks the first one.

ex.s: When we got to the cinema, the movie had already started.
He couldn't pay because he had lost his wallet.
By the time she called, I had gone to bed.
ex.n: by the time is a strong signal

uses.d: Like present perfect, but measured from a point in the past.

ex.s: Before 2020, I had never used a smartphone.
It was the best meal she had ever eaten.
They had met once before the party.

uses.d: Past perfect explains how things got that way.

ex.s: The ground was wet — it had rained all night.
I recognized him because we had worked together.
She was tired; she hadn't slept well.

mistakes.no: When I arrived, the train left.
mistakes.yes: When I arrived, the train had left.
mistakes.why: If the train left first, the earlier action needs past perfect.

mistakes.no: She had went home.
mistakes.yes: She had gone home.
mistakes.why: Had + past participle: go → gone.

mistakes.no: I had seen him yesterday.
mistakes.yes: I saw him yesterday.
mistakes.why: One single past event → past simple is enough.

tip: Only use past perfect when two past times are in play — it marks the earlier one. Just one event? Past simple.

q.q: The bus ___ by the time we reached the stop.
q.why: By the time → the earlier action takes past perfect.

q.q: I couldn't open the door because I ___ (forget) my keys.
She was nervous because she ___ a speech before.
q.why: Experience before a past moment → had never given.

q.sent: After they had ate lunch , they went for a walk .
The movie had started before we arrived
q.why: The earlier action takes had + started.

q.q: Which is correct?
opts: I had visited Japan last year.
I had visit Japan last year.
I have visited Japan last year.
q.why: One finished event with a past time → past simple.

q.q: By 10 p.m., everyone ___ (go) home.
q.why: Finished before that past point → had gone.

q.sent: When I called , she already had finish her homework .

title: Past Perfect Continuous
sub: Had been + V-ing — an action that had been going on for a while before another past moment.

tl.cap: A longer action that had been continuing up to a later point in the past.

form.p: subject + had been + verb-ing
ex: I had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
She was tired because she had been working all night.
They had been living there for years before they moved.

uses.d: An action that continued for a period up to a moment in the past.

ex.s: We had been driving for hours before we stopped.
He had been studying all day, so he was exhausted.

uses.d: Explains why something was true at that moment in the past.

ex.s: The ground was wet because it had been raining.
Her eyes were red — she had been crying.

uses.d: Add not to had; put had before the subject in questions.

ex.s: They hadn't been getting along for a while.

mistakes.no: I was waiting for an hour when he arrived.
mistakes.yes: I had been waiting for an hour when he arrived.
mistakes.why: Duration up to a past point → past perfect continuous.

mistakes.no: She had been work all night.
mistakes.yes: She had been working all night.
mistakes.why: Need been + verb-ing.

mistakes.no: We had been knowing them for years.
mistakes.yes: We had known them for years.
mistakes.why: Stative verbs (know) use past perfect, not the continuous.

tip: Two pasts: the longer, ongoing one takes had been + V-ing; the later, shorter one takes past simple (when he arrived).

q.q: I ___ for an hour when the bus finally came.
q.why: Ongoing duration before a past point → had been waiting.

q.q: She was tired because she ___ all night.
q.why: Reason for a past state → had been working.

q.q: The road was wet because it ___ (rain).
q.why: Cause of a past result → had been raining.

q.sent: They had been live there for years .
q.why: Need been + verb-ing: had been living.

q.sent: How long had you been waiting

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: He had been knowing her for years.
I had been reading before he called.
She had been work all day.
q.why: had been + V-ing; stative verbs don't take the continuous.

title: Used To
sub: Past habits and states that are no longer true.

form.p: subject + used to + base verb
ex: We didn't use to have a car.

uses.t: used to — a past habit that stopped
uses.d: Use used to + base verb for something that happened regularly in the past, but not now.

ex.s: I used to ride my bike to school.
We used to watch cartoons every Saturday.
He used to smoke, but he stopped.

uses.d: Also for a situation that was true before, but changed.

ex.s: There used to be a shop here.

uses.d: With didn't and in questions, drop the -d: didn't use to / Did you use to…?

ex.s: He didn't use to be so quiet.

mistakes.no: I use to play football.
mistakes.yes: I used to play football.
mistakes.why: In the positive form it's used to (with -d).

mistakes.no: I used to played tennis.
mistakes.yes: I used to play tennis.
mistakes.why: used to + base verb (play), not played.

mistakes.no: Did you used to live here?
mistakes.yes: Did you use to live here?
mistakes.why: After did, drop the -d: use to.

tip: used to + base verb = a past habit/state that isn't true now. But after didn't / did, drop the -d → 'use to'.

q.q: I ___ live in Taipei, but now I live in Tainan.
___ you use to play the piano?
Which is correct?
She ___ to have a cat. (past habit, positive)

q.sent: We used to live by the sea
He didn't used to like vegetables .
q.why: After didn't, drop the -d: didn't use to.

q.q: 'There used to be a cinema here' means…
opts: There was a cinema before, but not now.
q.why: used to = true before, not now.

q.sent: I use to walk to school every day .

zh: 過去時間詞 ago / last / yesterday
title: Past Time Words
sub: ago, last, yesterday — the time markers that go with the past simple.

form.p: …time + ago · last … · yesterday · in + past year

uses.d: Put ago AFTER a length of time. It means 'before now'.
Use last before night / week / month / year / Monday… No 'the', no preposition.
Other common past time markers.

mistakes.no: I saw him ago three days.
mistakes.yes: I saw him three days ago.
mistakes.why: ago comes AFTER the time: three days ago.

mistakes.no: We met in last week.
mistakes.yes: We met last week.
mistakes.why: No preposition with last: last week.

mistakes.no: She left yesterday night.
mistakes.yes: She left last night.
mistakes.why: Use 'last night', not 'yesterday night'.

tip: ago goes AFTER the time (two hours ago). last + week/night/year (no 'the', no 'in'). Say 'last night' (not 'yesterday night').

q.q: I moved here two years ___.
We had a test ___ week.
Which is correct?
He called me ___ night. (the night before)

q.sent: She arrived an hour ago
They got married in last summer .

q.q: Which sentence needs the past simple?
q.why: 'yesterday' is a past time word → past simple (saw).

q.sent: We came back yesterday night .

title: Stative Verbs
sub: Verbs of thoughts, feelings and senses — usually NOT used in the -ing form.

form.p: stative verbs stay simple, not continuous

uses.d: They describe a state, not an action: feelings (like, love, hate, want), thoughts (know, think, believe, understand) and belonging (have, own, belong).
With stative verbs, use the present simple even for 'now'.
A few verbs are stative OR active depending on their meaning.

ex.s: She has a car. / She's having lunch.

mistakes.no: I am knowing the answer.
mistakes.yes: I know the answer.
mistakes.why: know is stative — no -ing.

mistakes.no: She is wanting a coffee.
mistakes.yes: She wants a coffee.
mistakes.why: want is stative — use the simple form.

mistakes.no: I am liking this film.
mistakes.yes: I like this film.
mistakes.why: like is a feeling (stative) — no -ing.

tip: Feelings, thoughts and senses (like, know, want, believe, taste…) usually don't take -ing. Say 'I understand', not 'I am understanding'.

q.q: I ___ what you mean.
She ___ three languages.
Which sentence is correct?
This cake ___ delicious! (taste — a sense, it → ?)

q.sent: I don't believe this story
He is having two sisters .
q.why: have = possession here → stative → has (not 'is having').

q.q: Which verb can take -ing (as an action)?
q.why: 'think about' as an action can be continuous: I'm thinking about it.

q.sent: I am loving my new bike .
q.why: love is a feeling (stative) → love, not 'am loving'.

title: Present Perfect: For & Since
sub: Saying how long — for a length of time, since a starting point.

form.p: have/has + V3 + for + period / since + point

uses.d: Use for with a period (how long): for two hours, for a week, for years.

ex.s: He's had that car for a long time.

uses.d: Use since with a starting point (when it began): since 2010, since Monday, since I was a child.
Use How long + present perfect to ask about duration.

ex.s: How long has she worked there?

mistakes.no: I've been here since three days.
mistakes.yes: I've been here for three days.
mistakes.why: three days is a length → for.

mistakes.no: She's worked here for Monday.
mistakes.yes: She's worked here since Monday.
mistakes.why: Monday is a starting point → since.

mistakes.no: I live here for five years.
mistakes.yes: I've lived here for five years.
mistakes.why: For 'how long up to now', use the present perfect (have lived).

tip: for + how long (a period: for 3 days). since + when it started (a point: since Monday). Use them with the present perfect (have/has + V3).

q.q: I've known her ___ ten years.
q.why: ten years is a period → for.

q.q: He's lived in Japan ___ 2015.
___ have you studied English?
We've been waiting ___ an hour. (a period)
She's been sick ___ Monday. (a point)

q.sent: I've had this phone since two years .
q.why: two years is a period → for.

q.q: 'I've worked here since June' means I started…
opts: in June, and I still work here
q.why: since = the start point; I still work here now.

q.sent: They have been friends for they were kids .
q.why: 'they were kids' is a starting point → since.

zh: 未來式 be going to / will
title: Future: Going To vs Will
sub: Two futures with different jobs — plans and evidence vs promises and snap decisions.

tl.cap: Both point forward — the difference is when you decided.

form.p: be going to + verb   ·   will + verb
ex: I'm going to visit my aunt on Sunday.
I'll help you with those bags.
It's going to rain — look at the sky.

uses.d: You decided before speaking — the plan already exists.

ex.s: We're going to travel to Kenting in July.
She's going to study abroad next year.

uses.d: You can see or feel the cause right now.

ex.s: Look at those clouds — it's going to pour.
Careful! You're going to drop that.

uses.d: You decide at the moment of speaking — or you promise, offer or predict from opinion.

ex.s: The phone's ringing — I'll get it.

mistakes.no: I will to call you tonight.
mistakes.yes: I will call you tonight.
mistakes.why: Will is followed by the base verb — no to.

mistakes.no: She going to move next month.
mistakes.yes: She is going to move next month.
mistakes.why: Don't drop be: is / am / are going to.

mistakes.no: Look out! You will hit that pole!
mistakes.yes: Look out! You're going to hit that pole!
mistakes.why: Visible evidence → going to.

tip: Decided before speaking → going to. Deciding as you speak → will. Menus are the classic test: "I'll have the pasta."

q.q: A: We have no milk. B: Really? I ___ some on my way home.
q.why: A decision made right now → will.

q.q: Look at that long queue — we ___ for ages.
q.why: Prediction from evidence you can see → going to.

q.q: Don't worry, I ___ tell anyone your secret. (negative)
They ___ going to get married in spring.

q.sent: She is going to start a new job
I will to see the dentist tomorrow .
q.why: Will + base verb, never will to.

q.q: Which shows a plan decided earlier?
opts: I'm going to repaint my room this weekend.
q.why: Repainting this weekend is a pre-made plan → going to.

q.sent: He is going buy a scooter next month .
q.why: Going to needs to before the verb.

zh: 未來進行式與未來完成式
title: Future Continuous & Perfect
sub: Will be doing and will have done — painting a more precise future.

form.p: will be + V-ing   ·   will have + past participle
ex: This time tomorrow, I will be flying.

uses.t: Future continuous: in progress at a future time
uses.d: The action will be happening around that moment.

ex.s: At 8 p.m. tonight, we will be having dinner.
Don't call at noon — I'll be driving.
This time next week, they will be lying on a beach.

uses.t: Future perfect: finished before a future point
uses.d: Look back from a future deadline — the action will already be done.

ex.s: By 2030, the city will have built the new MRT line.
She will have finished the report before the meeting.
I will have saved enough by December.

uses.d: Will you be doing…? sounds softer than will you do…?

ex.s: Will you be using the printer this afternoon?
How long will you have been here by Friday?

mistakes.no: By next year, I will finish the course.
mistakes.yes: By next year, I will have finished the course.
mistakes.why: By + future point → future perfect.

mistakes.no: I will be finish soon.
mistakes.yes: I will be finishing soon.
mistakes.why: Will be + V-ing.

mistakes.no: She will have went home by then.
mistakes.yes: She will have gone home by then.
mistakes.why: Will have + past participle: gone.

tip: See by + a future time? That's the classic signal for will have + past participle.

q.q: This time tomorrow, we ___ over the Pacific.
q.why: In progress at that future moment → will be flying.

q.q: By Friday, I ___ (finish) all my exams.
q.why: Done before Friday → will have finished.

q.q: Don't visit at 9 — she ___ her online class.
q.why: In progress at 9 → will be having.

q.sent: By 2030 , he will have wrote three novels .
She will be working late tonight

q.q: Which is correct?
opts: By June, they will have moved house.
By June, they will moving house.
By June, they will have move house.
q.why: By + future → will have + past participle.

q.q: At midnight, most people ___ (sleep).
q.why: In progress at midnight → will be sleeping.

q.sent: We will had eaten before the show starts .

title: Future Perfect Continuous
sub: Will have been + V-ing — how long an action will have been going on by a future time.

tl.cap: An action continuing up to a point in the future — the focus is on the duration by then.

form.p: subject + will have been + verb-ing
ex: By next month, I will have been working here for ten years.
By 8 p.m., they will have been driving for six hours.
In May, we will have been living here for a decade.

uses.t: Duration up to a future point
uses.d: Says how long an action will have continued by a certain future time — usually with by and for.

ex.s: By July, she will have been teaching for 20 years.
At midnight, I will have been studying for eight hours straight.

uses.d: Explains why someone will feel or be a certain way at a future time.

ex.s: He'll be tired because he will have been working all day.
They'll be hungry — they will have been travelling since dawn.

mistakes.no: By June, I will work here for five years.
mistakes.yes: By June, I will have been working here for five years.
mistakes.why: How long, up to a future point → future perfect continuous.

mistakes.no: They will have been drive for hours.
mistakes.yes: They will have been driving for hours.
mistakes.why: Need been + verb-ing.

mistakes.no: By then she will have been knowing him for years.
mistakes.yes: By then she will have known him for years.
mistakes.why: Stative verbs (know) use future perfect, not the continuous.

tip: Use by + a future time with for + a length of time: By 2030, I will have been living here for ten years.

q.q: By next month, I ___ here for ten years.
q.why: How long, by a future point → will have been working.

q.q: By 8 p.m., they ___ for six hours.
q.why: Duration up to a future time → will have been driving.

q.q: At midnight, she ___ (study) for eight hours.
q.why: Duration by a future point → will have been studying.

q.sent: By June we will have been live here for a decade .
q.why: Need been + verb-ing: will have been living.

q.q: He'll be exhausted because he ___ all day.
q.why: Reason for a future state → will have been working.

q.q: Which time words fit the future perfect continuous?
q.why: by + a future time, for + a length of time.

title: Zero Conditional
sub: If + present, present — facts, habits and things that are always true.

form.p: If + present simple , … present simple
ex: If I drink coffee at night, I can't sleep.

uses.d: Whenever the condition happens, the result always follows.

ex.s: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
If the power goes out, the fridge stops.

uses.d: Your own always-true patterns work the same way.

ex.s: If I have free time, I read manga.

uses.d: If + present, then a command — very common in real life.

mistakes.no: If you will heat ice, it melts.
mistakes.yes: If you heat ice, it melts.
mistakes.why: No will in the if-part.

mistakes.no: If she eats seafood, she will always get a rash.
mistakes.yes: If she eats seafood, she gets a rash.
mistakes.why: Always true → present + present.

mistakes.no: If you heated ice, it melts.
mistakes.yes: If you heat ice, it melts.
mistakes.why: Zero conditional stays in the present.

tip: Both halves stay in present simple. Swap if for when — if the meaning barely changes, it's a zero conditional.

q.q: If you ___ water, it turns to steam.
If I ___ (eat) too much, I feel sleepy.
Ice ___ if you leave it in the sun.

q.sent: If it rain , the game stops .
If it snows the school closes

q.q: Which is a zero conditional?
opts: If you heat metal, it expands.
If I were you, I'd rest.
If she had studied, she'd have passed.
q.why: Always true, present + present → zero conditional.

q.q: If you don't water plants, they ___ (die).

q.sent: My eyes hurts if I read in the dark .

title: First Conditional
sub: Real future possibilities — if this happens, that will happen.

form.p: If + present simple, … will + verb
ex: You'll miss the bus if you don't hurry.

uses.d: Use it when the condition is realistic and quite possible.

ex.s: If you study tonight, you'll pass the quiz.
ex.n: present in the if-part, will in the result

ex.s: If the weather is nice, we'll have a picnic.
I'll be surprised if he arrives on time.

uses.d: First conditional is the natural shape of everyday deals and warnings.

ex.s: If you touch that pan, you'll burn yourself.
If you help me move, I'll buy you dinner.

uses.d: Unless means if … not. The result can also use can, might or an imperative.

mistakes.no: If it will rain, we'll cancel.
mistakes.yes: If it rains, we'll cancel.
mistakes.why: No will in the if-clause — present simple only.

mistakes.no: If you'll study, you pass.
mistakes.yes: If you study, you'll pass.
mistakes.why: Will belongs in the result clause.

mistakes.no: Unless you don't hurry, we'll be late.
mistakes.yes: Unless you hurry, we'll be late.
mistakes.why: Unless already contains the negative.

tip: The if-clause describes the condition in plain present; the will lives only in the result. Swapping the halves is fine — just add a comma when if comes first.

q.q: If she ___ hard, she'll get the scholarship.
If you heat ice, it ___.
You'll feel better if you ___ some rest. (get)
If we miss the train, we ___ a taxi. (take)

q.sent: If it rains we will cancel the picnic
If he will call , I'll let you know .

q.q: ___ you water this plant, it will die.
q.why: Unless = if you don't water it.

q.sent: If you study hard , you pass the exam .
q.why: The result of a first conditional needs will.

zh: 用現在進行式談未來安排
title: Future: Present Continuous
sub: Using 'be + -ing' for fixed future plans and arrangements.

form.p: subject + am / is / are + V-ing + future time
ex: She's flying to Tokyo on Friday.

uses.d: Use the present continuous for future plans you have already arranged (a time, a place, other people).

ex.s: I'm seeing the doctor at 3 p.m.

uses.d: A future time (tomorrow, tonight, on Friday…) makes it clear you mean the future, not now.

ex.s: I'm starting my new job next week.

uses.t: Present continuous vs will vs going to
uses.d: Present continuous for arranged plans; will for decisions/predictions; going to for intentions.

mistakes.no: I meet my friend tomorrow.
mistakes.yes: I'm meeting my friend tomorrow.
mistakes.why: For an arranged plan, use the present continuous.

mistakes.no: She is fly to Tokyo on Friday.
mistakes.yes: She is flying to Tokyo on Friday.
mistakes.why: be + V-ing: is flying.

mistakes.no: We are go to the concert tonight.
mistakes.yes: We are going to the concert tonight.
mistakes.why: be + V-ing: are going.

tip: Present continuous (be + -ing) also talks about the FUTURE — for plans you've already arranged, usually with a future time word (tomorrow, on Friday).

q.q: I ___ my grandparents this weekend. (an arranged plan)
What ___ you doing tonight?
Which best fits an already-arranged appointment?
opts: I will see the dentist someday.

q.q: They ___ getting married next month. (be)

q.sent: We are leaving on Sunday
She is fly to London tomorrow .

q.q: 'I'm meeting Sam at 6' means…
opts: I have arranged to meet Sam at 6.
q.why: present continuous for a fixed arrangement.

q.sent: I am start my new job next week .

title: Tenses Review
sub: Choosing the right tense — a mixed review of past, present and future.

form.p: let the time signal choose the tense

uses.d: Present simple for habits & facts (every day, usually); present continuous for right now.
Past simple for a finished time (yesterday, in 2019); present perfect for experience or 'up to now' (ever, for, since).

uses.t: Future: will / going to / present continuous
uses.d: will for decisions & predictions; going to for intentions; present continuous for arrangements.

mistakes.no: I have seen him yesterday.
mistakes.yes: I saw him yesterday.
mistakes.why: With 'yesterday' (a finished time), use the past simple.

mistakes.no: She works right now.
mistakes.yes: She's working right now.
mistakes.why: For 'right now', use the present continuous.

mistakes.no: I live here since 2015.
mistakes.yes: I've lived here since 2015.
mistakes.why: With 'since', use the present perfect.

tip: Let the time word choose the tense: every day → present simple; now → present continuous; yesterday → past simple; for/since → present perfect; tomorrow → will/going to/present continuous.

q.q: Listen! The baby ___ .
I ___ my homework an hour ago.
She ___ in this city since 2016.
We usually ___ dinner at seven.
Look at those clouds — it ___ going to rain. (be)
q.why: it is going to rain (prediction with evidence).

q.sent: I have watched a great film yesterday .

q.q: 'I've been to Japan' is which tense?

q.sent: They are knowing the answer .
q.why: know is stative → present simple: they know.

title: Comparatives & Superlatives
sub: Taller, more expensive, the best — comparing two things or picking the extreme.

form.p: adj-er + than   ·   the + adj-est   ·   more / the most + long adj

uses.d: Short adjectives add -er; long ones (2+ syllables) take more. Don't forget than.

ex.s: The test was more difficult than I expected.

uses.t: Superlatives: the extreme of a group
uses.d: Use the + -est or the most when comparing three or more.

ex.s: She is the fastest runner on the team.
That was the most interesting talk of the day.
It's the best beef noodle soup in the city.

uses.d: A few adjectives change completely; use as … as to say two things are equal.

ex.s: This café is as good as the famous one.

mistakes.no: This one is more cheaper.
mistakes.yes: This one is cheaper.
mistakes.why: Never combine more with -er.

mistakes.no: She is taller then me.
mistakes.yes: She is taller than me.
mistakes.why: Comparisons use than, not then.

mistakes.no: It's the goodest option.
mistakes.yes: It's the best option.
mistakes.why: Good is irregular: good → better → best.

tip: One syllable → -er / -est. Three or more → more / most. Two syllables? If it ends in -y (happy), use -ier; otherwise usually more.

q.q: This road is ___ than the highway.
It was ___ movie I've ever seen.
q.why: Superlative of a long adjective → the most.

q.q: My grades are ___ (good) than last semester.
August is the ___ (hot) month of the year.

q.sent: She is the smartest student in our class
This restaurant is more better than that one .
q.why: Better is already comparative — no more.

q.sent: He is older then his cousin .

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: She is as tall than me.
She is so tall as me.
She is as tall as me.

title: Quantifiers: Some & Any
sub: Some for positives and offers, any for negatives and most questions.

form.p: some + positive / offers   ·   any + negatives / questions

uses.d: Use some with plural and uncountable nouns when the amount isn't exact.
Any replaces some when the sentence is negative or asks a real question.

uses.t: Some in questions: offers and requests
uses.d: When you expect yes — offering or asking politely — keep some.

mistakes.no: I don't have some money.
mistakes.yes: I don't have any money.
mistakes.why: Negatives take any.

mistakes.no: Do you have some brothers?
mistakes.yes: Do you have any brothers?
mistakes.why: Real questions take any.

mistakes.no: There aren't any milk.
mistakes.yes: There isn't any milk.
mistakes.why: Milk is uncountable → isn't.

tip: Offering or requesting and expecting a yes? Use some, even in a question: "Would you like some more?"

q.q: Is there ___ bread left?
Would you like ___ coffee?
Sorry, we don't have ___ tables free right now.
I need to buy ___ new shoes.

q.sent: There isn't any sugar in my tea
She didn't bring some snacks to share .

q.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: Could I have a water anys?

q.sent: Do you have some questions for me ?

title: Linking Words
sub: However, although, therefore — making your ideas flow logically.

form.p: Although + clause , clause   ·   Clause . However , clause

uses.d: Although joins two clauses in one sentence; however starts a new one.

ex.s: Although the food was cheap, it tasted great.
The hotel was small. However, it was very clean.
Even though she was tired, she kept working.

uses.d: Formal cousins of so — great for writing.

ex.n: semicolon or full stop before it

ex.s: He missed the bus. As a result, he was late.
The evidence was weak; therefore, the case was dropped.

uses.d: Moreover, in addition and for example organize longer writing.

ex.s: The plan is cheap. Moreover, it is fast.
Many night markets are famous — for example, Raohe and Shilin.
She speaks three languages. In addition, she codes.

mistakes.no: Although it was late, but we kept talking.
mistakes.yes: Although it was late, we kept talking.
mistakes.why: Although and but — pick one, not both.

mistakes.no: However he was tired, he finished.
mistakes.yes: Although he was tired, he finished.
mistakes.why: However can't join two clauses inside one sentence the way although can.

mistakes.no: It was expensive, however, I bought it.
mistakes.yes: It was expensive. However, I bought it.
mistakes.why: However needs a full stop or semicolon before it.

tip: Although lives inside one sentence; however and therefore start a new one — with a comma right after them.

q.q: ___ the test was hard, most students passed.
q.why: Joining two clauses in one sentence → although.

q.q: It was freezing. ___, we still went hiking.
q.why: Contrast starting a new sentence → however.

q.q: He forgot his lines. ___, the show went well.

q.sent: She studied hard , however she failed the exam .
q.why: Inside one sentence, use but — or rewrite with although.

q.sent: Although it was raining we played outside
q.why: Although + clause, then the main clause.

q.q: Prices increased; ___, demand dropped.
q.why: The drop is a result → therefore.

q.q: The room is big. ___, it has a great view.

q.sent: She loves seafood . Therefore , she never eats fish .
q.why: The second idea contrasts — however, not therefore.

title: As … As Comparisons
sub: Saying two things are the same — or not the same — in some way.

form.p: as + adjective/adverb + as

uses.d: Use 'as + adjective + as' to say two things are equal in some quality.

ex.s: Tom is as tall as his brother.
This book is as good as that one.

uses.d: 'not as … as' means the first thing is less.

ex.s: The film wasn't as good as the book.

uses.d: Some 'as … as' phrases are fixed expressions.

mistakes.no: She is as taller as me.
mistakes.yes: She is as tall as me.
mistakes.why: Use the plain adjective between as … as: as tall as.

mistakes.no: He is not so tall than his dad.
mistakes.yes: He is not as tall as his dad.
mistakes.why: The pattern is not as … as (not 'than').

mistakes.no: This is as good than that.
mistakes.yes: This is as good as that.
mistakes.why: It's as … as, not 'as … than'.

tip: as + plain adjective/adverb + as = equal. not as … as = less than. Don't use the comparative (-er) or 'than' inside as … as.

q.q: My bag is ___ heavy ___ yours.
Which means 'today is cooler than yesterday'?
opts: Today is as hot as yesterday.
Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
Today is as cool than yesterday.
q.why: not as hot as = less hot = cooler.

q.q: Which is correct?
Please reply as soon ___ possible.

q.sent: She sings as well as a star
He is as strong than an ox .

q.q: 'I'm not as fast as you' means…
q.why: not as fast as = I'm slower → you're faster.

q.sent: This test is as easier as the last one .
q.why: Use the plain adjective: as easy as.

title: Too & Enough
sub: too = more than you want · enough = the right amount.

form.p: too + adjective · adjective + enough · enough + noun

uses.t: too + adjective = more than needed (a problem)
uses.d: 'too' means excessively — it's a bad thing.

ex.s: This coffee is too hot to drink.

uses.d: 'enough' means the right amount. It comes after an adjective or adverb.
'enough' comes BEFORE a noun.

mistakes.no: It's enough hot to swim.
mistakes.yes: It's hot enough to swim.
mistakes.why: enough goes AFTER an adjective: hot enough.

mistakes.no: He is too much tall.
mistakes.yes: He is too tall.
mistakes.why: Use too + adjective (no 'much'): too tall.

mistakes.no: I don't have money enough.
mistakes.yes: I don't have enough money.
mistakes.why: enough goes BEFORE a noun: enough money.

tip: too + adjective (a problem: too hot). adjective + enough (just right: hot enough). enough + noun (enough money).

q.q: This soup is ___ salty. I can't eat it.
Is it warm ___ to go outside?
We don't have ___ chairs for everyone.
She isn't tall ___ to reach the shelf.

q.sent: The box is too heavy to lift
He is enough old to vote .
q.why: enough goes after the adjective: old enough.

q.q: 'It's too small' means it is…
q.why: too small = a problem, smaller than you want.

q.sent: Do we have time enough ?
q.why: enough goes before a noun: enough time.

title: Either…or / Neither…nor
sub: Choosing between two — one or the other, or not either one.

form.p: either A or B · neither A nor B

uses.t: either … or = one of the two
uses.d: 'either A or B' means one of the two choices.

ex.s: You can have either cake or ice cream.
We'll meet either on Monday or on Tuesday.

uses.t: neither … nor = not one and not the other
uses.d: 'neither A nor B' means NOT A and NOT B. The verb stays positive.

uses.t: The verb agrees with the nearer subject
uses.d: When either/neither joins two subjects, the verb matches the one closest to it.

ex.s: Either the cats or the dog is hungry.
Neither he nor his friends were late.
Either you or she has the key.

mistakes.no: I don't like neither coffee nor tea.
mistakes.yes: I like neither coffee nor tea. / I don't like coffee or tea.
mistakes.why: neither is already negative — don't add another negative.

mistakes.no: You can have either cake nor ice cream.
mistakes.yes: You can have either cake or ice cream.
mistakes.why: either goes with or; neither goes with nor.

mistakes.no: Neither of them are ready.
mistakes.yes: Neither of them is ready.
mistakes.why: 'neither' is treated as singular → is (in careful English).

tip: either … OR (one of two). neither … NOR (not either one — the verb stays positive). Don't pair either with nor.

q.q: You can pay ___ by cash ___ by card.
___ Anna ___ Ben likes fish — they both hate it.
q.why: not Anna and not Ben → Neither … nor.

q.q: Which is correct?
opts: I don't like neither this nor that.
q.why: neither is already negative; keep the verb positive.

q.q: We can go ___ today or tomorrow.

q.sent: Neither he nor she was there
She speaks either French nor German .

q.q: 'Neither answer is correct' means…
opts: Not one of them is correct.
q.why: neither = not one and not the other.

q.sent: I don't like neither of them .
q.why: With don't, use either (no double negative).

title: Although & However
sub: Showing a contrast — 'but' in a more formal way.

form.p: Although + clause, clause · Sentence. However, sentence.

uses.t: although / even though — joins two clauses
uses.d: Use although at the start of a clause to show a surprising contrast. It connects two parts in one sentence.

ex.s: Although he was tired, he kept working.
We enjoyed it, although it was expensive.

uses.d: However shows a contrast between two separate sentences. It usually starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

ex.s: The plan was good. However, it was too expensive.
I like tea. However, I prefer coffee.

uses.d: but joins two ideas inside one sentence (less formal).

ex.s: I tried, but I couldn't do it.

mistakes.no: Although it was late, but we stayed.
mistakes.yes: Although it was late, we stayed.
mistakes.why: Don't use although and but together — one is enough.

mistakes.no: I was tired. Although, I finished.
mistakes.yes: I was tired. However, I finished.
mistakes.why: To start a new contrasting sentence, use However (not Although).

mistakes.no: However being tired, he worked.
mistakes.yes: Although he was tired, he worked.
mistakes.why: Although + a full clause (subject + verb).

tip: Although + clause, clause (one sentence). However + a new sentence, with a comma. Don't pair 'although' with 'but'.

q.q: ___ it was raining, we went for a walk.
The hotel was cheap. ___ , it was very clean.
Which sentence is correct?
opts: Although it was cold, but we swam.
Although it was cold, we swam.
However it was cold, we swam.
It was cold, although we swam however.

q.q: It looks difficult. ___ , it's actually easy. (contrast, new sentence)

q.sent: Although she was busy she helped me

q.q: ___ he is young, he is very wise. (contrast, one sentence)
'However' is usually followed by a…

q.sent: However being late , she caught the train .
q.why: Use Although + a clause (she was late), not However + -ing.

title: Transition Signals
sub: Signpost words that guide the reader — adding, contrasting, giving reasons and examples.

form.p: add · contrast · reason/result · example · sequence

uses.d: Use these to add points or show order.
Use these to show a difference or a consequence.
Introduce an example or wrap up.

mistakes.no: For example cats.
mistakes.yes: For example, cats.
mistakes.why: Put a comma after a transition signal at the start.

mistakes.no: In the other hand, it's small.
mistakes.yes: On the other hand, it's small.
mistakes.why: The phrase is 'On the other hand'.

mistakes.no: I was tired. Therefore I slept for however I was busy.
mistakes.yes: I was tired. Therefore, I slept.
mistakes.why: Use one clear signal; Therefore shows the result.

tip: Use signals to guide the reader: add (In addition, Also), contrast (However, On the other hand), result (As a result, Therefore), example (For example, Such as). A comma usually follows.

q.q: It was cheap. ___ , the food was delicious. (add a point)
It rained all day. ___ , the match was cancelled. (result)
I love fruit, ___ mangoes and grapes. (example)
The city is exciting. ___ , it's expensive. (contrast)
___ conclusion, I think it's worth visiting. (ending phrase)

q.sent: Firstly we will visit the museum
In the other hand , it is very quiet .
q.why: The phrase is 'On the other hand'.

q.q: Which signal shows a RESULT?
